title: Planarian evolutionary distance may reflect ease of shifting a shared patterning network

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Planarian evolutionary distance may reflect ease of shifting a shared patterning network

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The authors suggest that a core network of gene-regulatory elements and gap-junction-mediated signals may be shared among many planarians, with species differences tweaking its dynamics, so that evolutionary distance between planarian species may reflect how easily this network can be shifted into its different outcome states, as during gap junction inhibition.

fields.value: Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Emmons-Bell M 2015, Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms › 3. Discussion › 3.8. Stochastic Phenotypes and Evolutionary Implications

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The evolutionary distance among the planarian types may thus be expected to reflect the ease of shifting this network into its different potential outcome states (as occurs during GJC inhibition).

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Emmons-Bell M, Durant F, Hammelman J, Bessonov N, Volpert V, Morokuma J, Pinet K, Adams DS, Pietak A, Lobo D, Levin M, “Gap Junctional Blockade Stochastically Induces Different Species-Specific Head Anatomies in Genetically Wild-Type Girardia dorotocephala Flatworms”, International journal of molecular sciences (2015), doi:10.3390/ijms161126065; section “3. Discussion › 3.8. Stochastic Phenotypes and Evolutionary Implications”. Scope: Planarian species (Girardia, Dugesia, Schmidtea, Polycelis/Phagocata)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2015-girardia-21: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.45

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public sequences and the reported four-species experiment can examine a narrow correlation. They do not provide comparative perturbation thresholds or enough taxa to resolve the proposed evolutionary interpretation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across many planarian species, estimate phylogenetic distance and the perturbation magnitude needed to switch among homologous patterning outcomes, then test their relationship while controlling for drug uptake and morphology. Shared network components could be assessed from comparative genomic and expression data.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Perturbation-response data exist for very few species.

Head-shape frequency is only an indirect proxy for network shiftability.

Phylogeny, pharmacology, and morphology are confounded.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.2
data existence: 0.5
discriminating power: 0.35
operationalizability: 0.65
analysis feasibility: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public sequences can rebuild the distance half of the suggestion. The ease-of-shifting half is represented only by shape frequencies from one treated species, not by reciprocal perturbations across the clade. The phylogenetic ranking is therefore checkable now, and the network-evolution claim is not.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate phylogenetic distance from public planarian rRNA and compare it with the rate at which a standardized gap-junction block moves each species into the other species' head states. A monotone relation between distance and that transition rate would support the suggestion; no relation, or a relation that reverses after controlling for morphology, would weaken it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Only Girardia was pharmacologically shifted, so ease of transition is not measured in the other species.

A frequency ranking can track raw morphological similarity rather than network distance.
